newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel begins freeing Palestinian women prisoners.
newsitem.headline: Israel begins freeing Palestinian women prisoners.

text.p: Israel on Tuesday began freeing 31 Palestinian women prisoners, including two convicted killers, as part of its peace deals with the PLO, witnesses said.
A car left Hasharon prison in central Israel with the first to be freed: Lamya Maarouf, 32, a Brazilian citizen. Israeli and Palestinian officials said she would be deported to Brazil.
The release of 30 more women was expected later on Tuesday. Israel Radio said all would sign a paper promising to refrain from violence.
A PLO official said most of the freed women would be taken to the West Bank town of Ramallah where Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would welcome them.
"This is a great contribution to the peace process," Arafat told reporters in Ramallah.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, paying hospital visits in the north to soldiers wounded in Lebanon, said the promise to free the women was made originally by the previous Labour government.
"It's not a tactic, we are serious about fulfilling commitments, but we intend fully to see that there is an equal reciprocity on the other side," Netanyahu told reporters.

Israel has demanded the PLO keep its promise to change sections of the PLO charter calling for the destruction of the Jewish state, avoid political activity in Jerusalem and fight Palestinian guerrilla groups opposed to peace deals.
"Thirty-one Palestinian women will be released today, 25 from Hasharon prison and six from Neve Tirza prison," an Israeli police spokeswoman said.

Right-wing critics led by Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi called the decision to free the women immoral. The "Families of Victims of Arab Terror" group failed on Monday to persuade Israel's High Court to prevent the release.
Maarouf was arrested in 1986 for driving a car in which Israeli soldier David Manos was kidnapped. Manos was killed and Maarouf was sentenced to 25 years in jail.

Others due to be released included Abeer al-Wheidy, 27, arrested in 1992 for belonging to a cell of the PLO's mainstream Fatah faction which killed a Jewish settler from the settlement of Ofra near Ramallah and May Ghussein, 23, arrested in 1991 for security reasons.
Ghussein confessed to killing a Palestinian in jail suspected of collaborating with the prison authorities.
PLO official Hisham Abdel Razek said that after the release one Palestinian female would remain behind bars in Israel -- a 15-year-old arrested two weeks ago trying to stab an Israeli soldier.
He said 28 of the women were convicted of security offences and three were jailed for criminal activity unrelated to the Israeli-Arab conflict.
The release of female, sick and young prisoners was a commitment made in a deal signed by the previous government in September 1995 with the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Israel released some of the male sick and elderly prisoners but about 5,000 Palestinians are still in its prisons, Palestinian sources said.

Israeli President Ezer Weizman at first refused to pardon some of the women involved in deadly attacks against Israelis. The female prisoners he did pardon then chose to remain in prison in solidarity with their comrades.
An Israeli cabinet statement on Friday said the president had now decided to pardon all of the women.
Netanyahu pledged to carry out the prisoner releases in a deal with the PLO in January to hand over 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron to the Palestinians.
